rv.q: The Met supplied them all without apparently breaking a sweat.
It certainly didn’t usher in a new beginning with a rousing success, but it was neither a disaster nor a great controversy, and, low as that bar is set, the Met will probably be happy to take it.
The costumes could double for “Kismet,” and the whole look had a gaudy, metallic, 1970s vibe.
Mark Elder’s conducting, while inert, reveals moments of translucent beauty.
This timidly conceived staging, by the director Darko Tresnjak (“A Gentleman’s Guide to Love & Murder”) in his Met debut, somehow managed to be both gaudy and dull.
If so, things didn't quite work out as planned, particularly since the two aren't on stage together (or not in a clinch) for much of the opera and have smaller voices than are usually most effective.
That staging was intended to travel to the Met but the company opted instead for Tresnjak's limp take, which comes across as predictable and listless as a regional "instant opera" of the 1970s.

This enjoyable Samson, part pious oratorio, part campy revenge-girl seduction scheme, however may prove an audience-friendly popular success the company needs as it struggles to nightly fill its enormous theater.

The takeaway from this production is that the creative heads are still trying to figure out where they’re heading from an aesthetic standpoint with the insistence on traditional productions, dressed up as “modern” and “theatrical,” still the trademark.

cn.t: Critics find the Met's "Samson et Dalila" visually gaudy but dramatically hollow, with its over-the-top orientalist spectacle failing to compensate for lackluster staging and uneven performances from leads Alagna and Garanca.
